justice: The boulevard allocates substantial public space to all users through wide carriageways, a planted median, and continuous roadside green buffers.

Large street trees and landscaped medians improve environmental quality on both sides of the road, suggesting a relatively even distribution of greenery rather than concentrating amenities on only one frontage.

Accessibility is only moderate because no sidewalk, curb ramp, tactile paving, or marked pedestrian crossing is clearly visible in the image, limiting evidence of barrier-free access for all social groups.
safety: Multiple clearly painted lane markings and directional arrows organize vehicle movement and reduce lane ambiguity for drivers.
The planted central median and roadside planting strips create physical separation between opposing traffic streams, lowering head-on conflict risk.
Good daytime visibility, long sightlines, and modern streetlights support traffic safety, although the broad road width may still encourage higher vehicle speeds.
livability: Dense mature trees on both sides create a greener and calmer residential streetscape than a fully hardscaped arterial road.
Mid- and high-rise residential buildings along the left side indicate that the corridor serves daily living environments rather than only industrial or highway functions.
Livability is constrained by the road's very auto-oriented scale, with no visible benches, plazas, storefront activity, or pedestrian gathering spaces in the frame.
sustainability: Extensive tree canopy, hedges, and planted medians contribute to urban cooling, air-quality support, and ecological value.
The corridor landscaping appears continuous and well maintained, indicating sustained investment in green infrastructure rather than isolated decorative planting.
Sustainability is reduced by the dominance of multiple motor-traffic lanes and the absence of visible bus priority, bike lanes, or other strong low-carbon mobility infrastructure.
aesthetics: The avenue has a strong formal composition, with symmetrical rows of trees, curved light poles, and a landscaped median producing a coherent visual order.
Lush green vegetation on both sides softens the wide roadway and gives the street a parkway character.
The street appears clean, well maintained, and visually uncluttered, with orderly buildings and minimal signage clutter.
comfort: Thermal comfort is relatively good because large roadside trees provide substantial shade along the corridor edges and reduce heat exposure near sidewalks.
Physical comfort for pedestrians is uncertain because the image does not clearly show seating, shelters, or detailed sidewalk surfaces despite the generous green setting.
Psychological comfort benefits from the open sky view, low visible congestion, and orderly road environment, though the wide fast-moving roadway may feel intimidating for some users.
walkability: Walkability is limited because no clear sidewalk zone, curb ramps, zebra crossing, or pedestrian refuge crossing is visible in the image.
The street is very wide, so crossing distance would likely be long for pedestrians even though a planted median is present.
Tree cover and attractive greenery would make walking more pleasant at the edges, but the overall corridor design appears primarily oriented toward vehicle throughput rather than pedestrian movement.
bikeability: No dedicated bicycle lane, protected cycle track, or bike-specific pavement marking is visible on the roadway.
The multi-lane arterial layout likely exposes cyclists to higher motor-vehicle speeds and uncomfortable overtaking conditions.
Although the road surface is smooth and sightlines are long, the lack of cycling separation and support facilities keeps bikeability low.
